newsitem.title: UK: Investors eye political risk among Latam's giants.
newsitem.headline: Investors eye political risk among Latam's giants.

text.p: The vagaries of Latin American politics will play a decisive role in investor fortunes this year with the performance of heavyweight economies like Brazil and Mexico tempered strongly by political risk, investors say.

Rallies in Mexico and Brazil helped make Latin America the best performing region on a series of emerging market indices as New Year trading got under way, with Brazil in particular striding ahead for a second day running.
But fund managers say they are watching the political stories in these countries closely as they fine-tune their asset allocations for maximum return.
Emily McLaughlin, Latin American fund manager at Foreign & Colonial, singled out Brazil as F&C's market of preference in the region, with Mexico second despite its tricky politics.
But she said Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's efforts to win a constitutional amendment allowing him to stand for a second consecutive term would be a crucial market issue.

"For the region as a whole the main test will be the re-election of Cardoso," she said, as Brazil's Congress this week began a month-long extraordinary session to decide the fate of the president's re-election dream.

"We believe there's a 70 percent probability that Cardoso will be able to get that amendment through and that he in fact will benefit from it as the next president, which will be positive for Brazil," she said.
But the gap between domestic and foreign perceptions of his chances means there is a key investment opportunity now.

"I think the locals have virtually completely discounted (the amendment being passed) but the important thing is that international investors have not yet -- therefore there is scope for a lot more money to go flowing into that economy," McLaughlin said. "I can't tell you how important that is."
ING Barings, posting an overweight recommendation for Brazil in both the short and long term, said that markets had more factors to take into account looking ahead.

"With the re-election amendment riding high in congress, due to the good approval ratings of President Cardoso, the market has further to discount on reform passage, lower inflation and greater earnings growth into 1997," it said.
On Cardoso's re-election hangs the future of a reform process aimed at cementing low inflation and reducing Brazil's hefty fiscal deficit.
Mexico, meanwhile, goes into mid-term congressional elections in July with the ruling PRI, in power for 67 years, facing the likelihood of a defeat which it is unlikely to accept with good grace.
WestMerchant Capital Markets last week warned that the political turbulence surrounding the polls posed a major threat to the emerging country debt market this year.
ING Barings said it was cautiously optimistic over the Mexican economy in 1997, recommending an overweight position in the short term and modest underweight allocations in the long term.

But it told investors to expect headline-seeking activities by guerrilla groups, heated electoral campaigns and disputed election results over the course of the year, and warned of their impact on debt and equity markets.
"There is the risk of spillover from political developments on the financial markets, especially before and after the July elections," it said.
While McLaughlin is relatively bullish on Mexico, at least in the first quarter, she said the ability to monitor shifting sentiment among foreign investors would be vital.
"The markets don't like uncertainty -- people will start to anticipate the mid-term elections in July and that will cause nerves -- it's a question of when they start to get the jitters," she said.
